MESSAGE:
Hi. I'm off to Lisbon next week for a three-day work trip, my first time in Portugal, and I want to travel carry-on only this time, after the airline lost my case in the spring.

Could you suggest three things to do in Lisbon on a free evening? And how do I say "thank you" in Portuguese? Is it different depending on who's saying it? And is tipping expected in restaurants there, or is that more of an American thing?

My wheeled bag measures 56 × 36 × 23 cm including the wheels and handle, and packed it weighs 9 kg. Will it meet the carry-on limit?

Also, recommend a packing approach: rolling or folding for work shirts? I need a short out-of-office message that's professional but not stiff, since most of my contacts are clients rather than colleagues. And what's a good colour for a luggage tag so it's easy to spot? I'm flying back on the Friday evening, straight after a full day of meetings, so anything that makes the return journey less stressful is welcome.

Thanks a lot.

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest three things to do in Lisbon in the evening
2. Explain how to say 'thank you' in Portuguese and whether it varies by speaker
3. Say whether tipping is expected in Lisbon restaurants
4. Determine whether a 56 x 36 x 23 cm, 9 kg bag meets the carry-on limit  KEY: Missing datum: the airline (and fare type) is not stated, and carry-on size/weight limits vary by airline and fare, so this cannot be confirmed. Should ask which airline/fare and illustrate: under a common 55 x 40 x 20 cm limit the bag fails (56 > 55 length, 23 > 20 depth); under a 56 x 45 x 25 cm limit it fits; weight limits range roughly 7-10 kg, so 9 kg may exceed a 7 or 8 kg limit.
5. Recommend rolling vs folding shirts
6. Write a short out-of-office message
7. Suggest a luggage tag colour

ANSWER:
Good call going carry-on only after losing a case. Here's everything, starting with the bag, because that one has a catch.

## Will your bag meet the carry-on limit?

**It depends entirely on the airline and the type of ticket.** Some airlines will accept it and some won't. Here are typical limits on the Lisbon route. Policies change, so check your airline's own page:

| Airline (typical cabin bag) | Size limit | Weight | Your bag (56 × 36 × 23, 9 kg) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TAP Air Portugal, economy | 55 × 40 × 20 cm | 8 kg | ❌ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep, 1 kg over |
| Lufthansa group | 55 × 40 × 23 cm | 8 kg | ❌ 1 cm too long, 1 kg over |
| British Airways | 56 × 45 × 25 cm | 23 kg | ✅ Fits |
| easyJet, large cabin bag (paid or included in some fares) | 56 × 45 × 25 cm | 15 kg | ✅ Fits |
| Ryanair, Priority (paid) | 55 × 40 × 20 cm | 10 kg | ❌ 1 cm too long, 3 cm too deep |

Two things to check on your booking:

1. **Your fare type.** Many basic fares only include a small bag that fits under the seat. A wheeled case like yours may need to be added as a paid extra.
2. **The exact numbers.** If your airline's limit is 55 cm, the extra centimetre and the extra depth could mean your case is put in the hold at the gate. That's exactly what you want to avoid.

If your airline's limit is 8 kg, take out about 1 kg: wear your bulkiest shoes and jacket on the plane.

## Three things to do on a free evening

1. **Sunset at a miradouro (viewpoint).** Miradouro da Senhora do Monte or Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara give you sweeping views over the city and the river.
2. **Fado in Alfama.** Have dinner at a small fado house in the old Alfama district to hear Portugal's traditional music live. Book ahead if you can.
3. **Dinner in Bairro Alto or Príncipe Real.** These neighbourhoods have lively streets, good restaurants and bars, and they're easy to walk around.

If you only have a couple of hours, the **Time Out Market** at Cais do Sodré is a quick way to try a lot of Portuguese food in one place.

## Saying "thank you"

**Obrigado** if you're a man, **obrigada** if you're a woman. It depends on *the gender of the person speaking*, not who you're thanking. "Muito obrigado/a" means "thank you very much."

## Tipping

It's not expected the way it is in the US. In sit-down restaurants, rounding up or leaving about **5–10% for good service** is appreciated but optional. In cafés and bars, leaving small change is plenty. Check the bill first to see whether a service charge has already been added.

## Packing work shirts

**Fold them.** Rolling suits casual clothes and knits, but folding (shirts buttoned, folded around a stiff card or each other) creases crisp shirts less. Hang them up as soon as you arrive. Hanging them in the bathroom while you take a hot shower lets the steam release most creases.

## Out-of-office message

> Thank you for your message. I'm travelling for work from [date] to [date] with limited access to email, but I'll reply as soon as I can when I'm back on [return date].
>
> If your query is urgent, please contact [name] at [email/phone], who will be happy to help.
>
> Best regards,
> [Your name]

## Luggage tag colour

**Neon orange or bright lime yellow.** They stand out against the sea of black and navy bags. A tag is useful even with carry-on only, in case your bag is put in the hold at the gate.

## Making Friday's return easier

- **Check in online and download your mobile boarding pass** on Thursday night.
- **Pack Friday morning before you check out,** and leave your bag at hotel reception. Most hotels will store it for the day, so you can pick it up after your meetings.
- **Allow plenty of time at the airport.** Lisbon Airport is busy and security queues can be long, especially on Friday evenings, so aim to arrive about 2 hours before departure. The metro's red line goes directly to the airport, or Uber and Bolt are widely used.
- **Keep liquids in a clear bag at the top of your case** (100 ml containers), so security is quick.

Have a great trip.
